prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, and for bringing them to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B015 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. After the full exchange I am more, not less, certain of the record, and the chair's questions did not turn up a new objection to the physics. The original idea is Katori's: a lattice at the magic wavelength in which the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once without perturbing the line. He also made the first strontium lattice clock. The second step is Ye's group. They took the instrument to the 10^-18 regime with a fully characterised systematics budget, and used it to measure gravitational redshift across millimetres and to study many-body (spin-exchange) effects in the clock. Both steps were confirmed in other laboratories (RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL), and the clock comparisons agree. I regard that as the experimental verification the Physics Prize requires, and I can say with confidence who did the original work. On the chair's first question I would answer that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. Combs gave a way to count optical cycles, and Wineland's prize was for controlling single quantum systems. The idea that a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held in a lattice without shifting the transition is new, and so is the many-body regime it opens. The citation should say that explicitly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that this is an invention and a measurement achievement more than a surprise from nature, and that a new phase of matter (B003) or a new observational window (B014) is a different order of discovery. I take that seriously, but the Physics Prize is for discovery or invention, and the original experiment, not the most spectacular one, is what I am asked to identify. Second, the SI second has not been redefined. I do not think the committee should wait for a metrology-body decision, because the scientific case already rests on the reproduced results, and a later redefinition would only add to it. Third, the credit is not perfectly bounded: Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko, and the ion-clock groups (Al+, Yb+) all contributed, and Ye's stability rests partly on cavities and combs built by others. The two-name credit is a judgement about the original idea and the decisive demonstration, not a claim that nobody else mattered, and the citation should name lattice clocks specifically so that it does not read as a statement about all of timekeeping.

responses.point: Lindroth warns that the citation must not imply that lattice clocks alone define the state of the art, since ion clocks compete at similar accuracy, and she also admits the case is invention and measurement rather than surprise.
responses.response: I agree with the first point, and it is the main reason my wording is limited to 'optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping' and does not say 'atomic timekeeping' in general. I do not want the citation to appear to rank platforms. On the second point I do not think admitting that this is invention rather than surprise weakens the case under our statutes, since invention is explicitly in scope. I would not accept widening the credit to Rosenband or the ion-clock groups, because that story belongs to the 2012 lineage and would also break the three-person cap. The proper answer to the chair's question on Lemonde and Takamoto is that they contributed to a programme that Katori initiated and Ye took to its limit. The original proposal and the first demonstration are documented, and I am less sure of the record for the others.

responses.point: Eriksson still weighs B003 against B015 as not fully settled, saying the depth of a new state of matter competes with B015's broad support and clean attribution, and he would keep Xue alongside Kane and Molenkamp.
responses.response: This is the comparison I took longest over, as B003 was my own first choice at opening, and I agree that the physics is deep. What decides it for me is the attribution, not the physics, and your own case against names the reason: Mele, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal are outside the three names, and Zhang has died. I also share your view that the QSH and QAH results are separate experiments, so the citation reads as a bundle of two achievements. If the committee prefers Kane and Molenkamp alone, I would still worry about Mele. I agree with you that broad support is not a substitute for merit. But here it coincides with a record I can state precisely, whereas for B003 I would not be sure that I had identified the right people. I keep B003 as my first alternative and I would revisit it if the committee can settle the credit.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B014 (Halzen and Karle) as a new observational window and says the case rests on the diffuse flux, not on source identification, while accepting that B015 may be the easier prize to defend.
responses.response: I accept that the diffuse flux is a real discovery and that several channels give independent support, which answers my round-1 concern about confirmation from a single analysis. I also accept the framing that the prize would be for the flux and neutrino astronomy and not for TXS 0506+056. What remains for me is the question of individuals. I would need to be absolutely sure that Halzen and Karle are the decisive contributors from a collaboration of hundreds, in the light of AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and ANTARES, and I do not think that has been documented to that standard. I also note that the source picture is only beginning (two individually significant sources). So B014 stays as an alternative, and not as my preferred prize. If the committee were to resolve the attribution, I would take it seriously for a later year.

responses.point: Kroll flags his year in John Hall's laboratory as an indirect link to the B015 milieu and does not think it requires recusal, and he notes that Ye's role rests partly on combs and cavities built by others.
responses.response: Having read the disclosure, I see no reason for him to recuse. He reports no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and a PhD-era connection to the laboratory that trained Ye is the sort of general proximity that every metrology-adjacent member would have. I would suggest that the committee records it and moves on. Because Ye's contribution builds on combs and cavities, I would also keep the citation on the lattice clock itself and its 10^-18 performance, so that we do not appear to be rewarding the earlier comb work a second time.

uncertainties: Whether the other members accept that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, in view of the objections by Mehlig, Lindroth and Eriksson that it can be read as refinement.
Whether the committee should wait for the SI second redefinition. I believe not, but I have no specific information on its timing.

Whether the boundary of the credit at Katori and Ye is fair to Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko. I think so for the original idea and the decisive demonstrations, but I have not verified every priority date.
Whether the B003 credit (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Xue, Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) could be resolved without injustice. If it could be, my ranking might change in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I work in electron microscopy at Chalmers and have no documented collaboration or institutional link with Katori or Ye, so I see no conflict on B015. I am a Chalmers colleague of Johansson, who has flagged a possible recusal on B039, which is not my preferred part. I have a general connection to the condensed-matter and materials community relevant to B003, B030 and B018, which I regard as a field proximity and not a personal link to any credited person. Having read Kroll's disclosure about John Hall's laboratory, I do not think it requires him to step back from the B015 discussion.
